title: The piRNA pathway mediates transcriptional silencing of LTR retrotransposons in ovaries and somatic tissues of Aedes mosquitoes.
data_url: https://github.com/vanrijlab/Taskopru_Piwi6 (code + transposon consensus FASTA, MIT licence; archived at Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.21803963); supplementary Tables S12-S14 in the article's supplementary zip; raw reads at NCBI SRA PRJNA1470531 / PRJNA1173503 / PRJNA989754

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and parsed all three supplementary spreadsheets (3,036 and 3,044 rows of DESeq2 output over transposon families; 1,723 transposon rows of small-RNA counts), read the column definitions out of the 26-page supplementary PDF, and downloaded the 10.5 MB transposon consensus FASTA from the authors' GitHub (3,098 sequences, 501-14,783 bp). Verified 3,035 of 3,036 spreadsheet names match FASTA headers exactly, 0 duplicate identifiers, 943 of 3,036 rows have no adjusted p-value, 226 of 1,723 small-RNA rows are zero counts, and computed label statistics myself: among well-measured families (mean normalized count >50) the fold-change spread is small (variance 0.37 log2 units, 555 of 1,856 families exceed twice their own standard error), rank correlation between Piwi6-bound small-RNA load and the two chromatin/polymerase fold changes is 0.00 and -0.08, transposon superfamily alone explains 5% and 2% of label variance, and a 21-mer MinHash clustering of the 3,098 sequences gives 2,998 clusters (largest 4 members), i.e. the sequence library is nearly non-redundant.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: That the RNA-seq experiment covered 2,533 transposon sequences with 206 differentially expressed (145 up, 61 down, 19 up >16-fold) - I could not check this because that differential-expression table is shown only in Figure 3A/B and is not provided as a file. Also taken from the text: numbers of replicates (three for RNA-seq, two for CUT&Tag and PRO-seq) and the claim that H3K9me3 is depleted and RNA polymerase II increased at the new endogenous retrovirus AalERV1.

a1_downloadable.note: All three supplementary spreadsheets and the transposon consensus FASTA downloaded without login; GitHub code/annotation repo is MIT-licensed and archived on Zenodo. Verified by opening every file.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: For the tabulated labels yes: 'log2FoldChange' (knockout vs wild-type) is a column in two tables and raw/normalized small-RNA counts plus a ratio column in the third. Caveat verified in the files: the headline label the paper is about - which transposon families go up in messenger RNA after Piwi6 knockout - is NOT in any file and would have to be rebuilt from raw reads.

a3_inputs_present.note: Input DNA sequences are present: the authors' repo ships TE_repeat_Aealb_all.fa with 3,098 consensus sequences whose headers match 3,035 of 3,036 spreadsheet rows exactly (checked by set intersection). No identifier lookups needed.

a4_units_stated.note: Supplementary PDF defines every column: mean of DESeq2-normalized counts, log2 fold change (knockout vs wild-type), standard error, Wald statistic, raw p-value, Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value; small-RNA table states raw counts, counts normalized per million microRNAs, and a ratio.

a5_enough_rows.note: 3,036 and 3,044 transposon families with fold changes, 1,723 with small-RNA counts, 1,856 well-measured (mean count >50). Verified by reading the files.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~0.02 GB (three spreadsheets ~1 MB total plus a 10.5 MB FASTA)
a6_fits_laptop.note: Everything fits in memory; no GPU needed for a k-mer baseline. Only the raw reads in SRA are large, and they are not needed for the tabulated labels.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Row counts (3,036 / 3,044 / 1,723) differ from the paper's 2,533 RNA-seq transposons, but those are different assays, so no contradiction. Real trap found: the file named 'Table 12' shows AalERV1 fold change +4.65 while its caption says Table S12 is H3K9me3, which contradicts the paper's figure showing H3K9me3 depletion at AalERV1 - the two files appear swapped relative to their captions. Resolvable from the AalERV1 direction, so not fatal, but it is a silent sign-flip waiting to happen.

a8_label_provenance.note: Labels trace to physical measurements (CUT&Tag sequencing for histone mark and polymerase occupancy, small-RNA sequencing after immunoprecipitation), summarized by DESeq2 - not another model's predictions. Residual concern: counts over highly similar repeat consensus sequences depend on how multi-mapping reads were assigned, which is itself a function of sequence; the knockout-versus-wild-type ratio largely cancels this.

B1.why: Three spreadsheets plus a FASTA from a separate repo; exact-key join verified (3,035/3,036 matched).

B2.why: Tables 12/13 parse cleanly; small-RNA table has merged headers and summary rows mixed into the data block.

B3.why: Each assay normalized by authors, but histone, polymerase and small-RNA labels are not comparable across assays.

B4.why: 943 of 3,036 rows have no adjusted p-value (independent filtering); 226 of 1,723 small-RNA rows are zero; easy to drop.

B5.why: Zero duplicate transposon identifiers in all three tables, checked directly in the files.

B6.why: Every column defined in the supplementary PDF, but file-to-caption assignment contradicts the paper's figures.

C1.why: A null result is uninterpretable: labels span only ~0.6 log2 units and the mechanistic predictor is uncorrelated with them.

C2.why: Searched: piRNA-vs-not classifiers and TEclass2 superfamily classifier exist; none predicts per-family silencing response.

C3.why: Nobody has modelled this data, but the payoff is thin: one cell line, one gene, one species.

C4.why: Current method is a CRISPR knockout cell line plus four sequencing assays per species - months of lab work.

C5.why: Obvious dummies exist and I computed them (superfamily mean explains 2-5%); no published model number to beat.

D1.why: Nucleotide Transformer v2 multispecies and DNABERT-2 are open-weight DNA backbones matching 0.5-15 kb sequences.

D2.why: 3,098 sequences of median 2.3 kb need chunked embedding on CPU; hours, not minutes, but cacheable once.

D3.why: Nucleotide Transformer v2 weights are non-commercial (CC-BY-NC-SA); data itself is MIT-licensed code plus journal supplement.

E1.why: Grouped split available: 2,998 k-mer clusters and 10 superfamilies computed from the provided FASTA.

E2.why: 10 superfamilies, largest groups LTR 871 and LINE 196 families among small-RNA-covered rows.

E3.why: Already computed global-mean and per-superfamily-mean baselines from the files (R-squared 0.02-0.05).

E4.why: Per-row standard error from two replicates is a column; median error variance 0.067 vs label variance 0.374.

E5.why: AalERV1 and LTR Gypsy family-3394 must rank top; superfamily should be predictable from sequence as a plumbing check.

E6.why: Label shuffling and feature ablation trivial on a 3,000-row table.

E7.why: No second tabulated dataset; comparable Aedes aegypti or Drosophila data exists only as raw reads needing reprocessing.

E8.why: No published model number for this task, and the paper's own RNA-seq differential-expression table is not provided.

G1.why: Only custom RepeatModeler names like 'TE@ltr-1_family-3394@LTR_Gypsy'; no Dfam accession or genome coordinates in the tables.

G2.why: Dfam (transposon family database) is plausible as a partner but joining needs sequence alignment, not an identifier.

G3.why: Alignment-based matching to Dfam or other mosquito libraries is one-to-many and needs an identity threshold decision.

G4.why: Cross-species question (do silenced families share features across Aedes and Drosophila) is real but needs raw-data reprocessing.

H1.why: All 3,036 families reported including the ~2,300 unaffected ones; negatives are present in the files.

H2.why: One cell line (U4.4), one species, one knocked-out gene, two to three replicates.

H3.why: Honest claim statable in one sentence (see honest_claim_h3).

H4.why: Paper states replicate numbers, assays and thresholds explicitly; gaps are visible to a reader.

I1.why: The van Rij lab and the arbovirus-vector piRNA community exist, but no one is waiting for this predictor.

I2.why: A ranked list of candidate Piwi6-target families could nominate elements for follow-up; marginal effect on their plans.

I3.why: Precision among top-ranked families roughly matches 'which element to test next', but no fixed decision threshold exists.

I4.why: The real driver is whether a family has copies inside a piRNA cluster - a sequence alignment lookup, not machine learning.

J1.why: Grouped splits, a DNA backbone, cached embeddings and honest negative controls - the ML skills on the wishlist.

J2.why: piRNA and transposon biology is specialized; sanity-checking predictions needs someone in that field.

J3.why: A cleaned sequence-plus-label table is shareable even if no model works, but it is small and of narrow interest.

J4.why: Tiny data makes a two-week budget plausible, but no budget is committed anywhere.

J5.why: No kill date or condition written down for this candidate.

existing_models.name: TEclass2 (transformer classifier of transposon consensus sequences, Biology 2026)
existing_models.score_and_split: Classifies consensus sequences into 16 transposon superfamilies; reported on held-out consensus sequences, no silencing-response task
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Classification of fragmented and unknown consensus sequences remains hard; expression or regulation is not addressed

existing_models.name: piRNA identification predictors (piRNN convolutional network; LSTM4piRNA; TranspoPred ensemble)
existing_models.score_and_split: Report AUC up to ~0.99 on Drosophila transposon-derived piRNA versus non-piRNA classification, mostly random splits of small-RNA sequences
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Performance drops in mammals and depends on negative-set construction

backbone.name: Nucleotide Transformer v2 multispecies (open weights) or DNABERT-2, with mean-pooled embeddings and a linear or gradient-boosted head; simple 4-6-mer composition as the honest baseline
backbone.hardware: 16 GB laptop CPU; 3,098 sequences of median 2.3 kb need chunked embedding, estimated several hours once
backbone.licence: Nucleotide Transformer v2 weights CC-BY-NC-SA (non-commercial); data: journal supplement plus MIT-licensed repo

integration.partner_dataset: Dfam transposon family database (and mosquito transposon libraries from Aedes aegypti)
integration.join_key: No shared identifier - would require sequence alignment (BLAST/MMseqs2) between consensus sequences
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Do the transposon families silenced by the piRNA pathway in Aedes albopictus share sequence features with those silenced in other mosquitoes and in flies, or is each species' silenced set idiosyncratic?

controls.positive_control: The paper's own standout element AalERV1 and LTR Gypsy family-3394 must rank at the top of the predicted-response list; separately, predicting transposon superfamily from sequence must work near-perfectly as a plumbing check
controls.negative_control: Shuffle the fold-change labels within superfamily and confirm collapse to the per-superfamily mean; replace embeddings with random vectors of the same shape
controls.external_validation: None available as a table - comparable Aedes aegypti Piwi4/Piwi5 knockdown or Drosophila piwi knockdown data exists only as raw sequencing reads that would need reprocessing with the same pipeline

honest_claim_h3: From a transposon family's consensus DNA sequence, the model would predict how its histone H3K9me3 mark, RNA polymerase II occupancy and Piwi6-bound small-RNA load change in one Aedes albopictus cell line (U4.4) when one of four PIWI genes is knocked out, measured in two to three replicates - not whether the element is silenced in mosquitoes generally.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a transposon's own DNA sequence to predict how strongly the cell's small-RNA defence system targets and silences it.
plain_idea.train_on: One consensus DNA sequence per transposon family (3,098 sequences, 501-14,783 base pairs, median 2.3 kb) from the authors' repository, joined by exact name to 3,036 rows of measurements; about 1,856 families are well enough measured to use.
plain_idea.predict: Three measured quantities per family: change in the repressive histone mark H3K9me3 and in RNA polymerase II occupancy after knocking out the Piwi6 gene (both from CUT&Tag sequencing, two replicates, summarized as log2 fold changes), and how many Piwi6-bound small RNAs map to that family (one immunoprecipitation sequencing library each for Piwi6, a mutant, and a control).
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Mosquito-biology labs studying how Aedes mosquitoes keep jumping genes quiet would learn whether a family's sequence alone says if the piRNA defence system targets it, which would let them pick follow-up elements without a knockout experiment; even a failure would quantify how little family-level sequence explains.

ml_idea: Predict, from each transposon family's consensus DNA sequence (embedded with an open DNA language model such as Nucleotide Transformer v2 or scored by simple k-mer composition), the family's Piwi6-bound small-RNA load and its change in H3K9me3 and RNA polymerase II occupancy after Piwi6 knockout, evaluated on k-mer-clustered and superfamily-held-out splits against per-superfamily-mean baselines. The data supports it mechanically but not substantively: I verified that Piwi6-bound small-RNA load is rank-uncorrelated with both chromatin responses (0.00 and -0.08) and that superfamily alone explains only 2-5% of label variance, so the most likely outcome is a model indistinguishable from the dummy baseline with no way to tell biology from noise.

effort.compute_note: Estimated from file sizes I actually opened (about 1 MB of spreadsheets, 10.5 MB FASTA) and from the 21-mer MinHash clustering I ran over all 3,098 sequences, which took a couple of minutes on this laptop; the 8-hour embedding figure is an estimate for chunked CPU inference of ~3,100 sequences of median 2.3 kb through a Nucleotide Transformer checkpoint, not timed.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Already done: rank-correlate Piwi6-bound small-RNA load (Table S14) against the two knockout-versus-wild-type fold changes (Tables S12/S13) and compute how much variance transposon superfamily explains. Results were 0.00 / -0.08 and 2-5%, which is the kill.

verdict_reason: The files are genuinely open and model-ready - 3,036 labelled transposon families joined by exact name to 3,098 consensus sequences, under 12 MB, MIT-licensed, zero duplicates, all columns documented - and I verified all of that by opening them. It dies on the question, not the data. The label the paper is actually about (which families are de-repressed in messenger RNA after Piwi6 knockout; 206 of 2,533) exists only inside Figure 3 and would have to be rebuilt from raw sequencing reads. What is tabulated are chromatin and polymerase fold changes spanning only about 0.6 log2 units, plus single-library small-RNA counts with no replicates, and I measured that the mechanistic predictor (Piwi6-bound small-RNA load) has essentially zero rank correlation with those responses (0.00 and -0.08) while superfamily explains 2-5% of their variance. With one cell line, one species, one knocked-out gene, no second dataset for external validation, and a mechanism that in practice reduces to 'does this family have copies inside a piRNA cluster' (an alignment lookup, not machine learning), a null result could not be distinguished from assay noise. Part B scores 7 of 12, C scores 5 of 10 and I scores 3 of 8 - below threshold on all three.
